title: A Disclosed Sale, a Sealed Warrant and a Closed File: the February 2020 Senate Stock Sales on the Court Record
participants: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (Chief Judge Beryl A. Howell)
U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit
Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: On 13 February 2020 Senator Richard Burr and his wife sold stocks valued, on the mandatory Senate filings, at between $628,000 and $1.72 million. The market fell sharply soon afterwards as the pandemic became general knowledge. The sale is on the record because a statute requires it to be: the STOCK Act obliges the filing of a periodic transaction report within 30 days of notification and in no case later than 45 days after the trade.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The asymmetry at issue is structural rather than contrived. The Senator sat on the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions and, as the D.C. Circuit records, "had received briefings on the pandemic in his capacity as a Senator" shortly before those sales. Congress had legislated against exactly this in 2012, affirming that its own members "are not exempt from the insider trading prohibitions arising under the securities laws" and writing into the Securities Exchange Act a duty of trust and confidence owed to the Congress, the Government and the citizens of the United States.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog here was not in the market; it was over the investigation. A warrant to search the Senator’s cellphone issued under seal on 13 May 2020. For more than a year of litigation the Department of Justice would not confirm that any such warrant, or any investigation, existed — forcing the district court to reason about "hypothesized search warrant materials" and the court of appeals to do the same. What finally broke the silence came from a different agency: the SEC’s October 2021 application in the Southern District of New York to enforce a subpoena on the Senator’s brother-in-law disclosed the investigation, its parallel criminal track, and some of the underlying telephone records.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: No charge was ever brought. The Department closed its criminal review and told the Senator so in January 2021; his statement was four sentences long and ended "The case is now closed." The district court’s 2022 opinion describes the matter twice as a closed investigation "that resulted in no prosecution of former Senator Burr". What the trades were worth, against what the holdings would have been worth a month later, appears in no document read here.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment in this dossier is a sealing order, and it was partly undone in public by a judge. On remand, the Department acknowledged the warrant’s existence on 24 May 2022 and filed a heavily redacted version. Chief Judge Howell granted continued sealing for third-party privacy and investigative technique, and refused it for the rest: redactions "intended to preserve the due process interests of investigative targets against whom the probable cause allegations in the warrant were made without any criminal charges being brought must be disclosed", with named paragraphs of the supporting affidavit ordered opened by 5 September 2022. The mechanism the atlas usually finds closing over a case here partly reopened it — and only because a newspaper litigated for eighteen months.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Ethics in Government Act disclosure regime, as amended in 2012 by the STOCK Act — a self-imposed reporting duty on the legislature, enforced through publication rather than through an outside auditor.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A worked precedent on both halves of the problem: that the securities laws reach a sitting senator through a duty of trust and confidence owed to the citizens, and that search warrant materials in a closed, uncharged investigation of a public official are judicial records whose sealing must be justified line by line.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The same statute produces both the suspicion and the defence. Disclosure is what made the February 2020 sales visible at all; the absence of any charge is what the disclosure regime, having worked, leaves behind. Each side of the public argument now cites the half of that record it prefers.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That senators were briefed on the coming pandemic in January 2020, quietly dumped their portfolios before the public knew, and were protected from any consequence by their own institution.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The protection is the part that fails hardest. The sales are known because a law Congress passed about itself required them to be filed and published; the FBI obtained a warrant for a sitting senator’s cellphone within three months; the Securities and Exchange Commission ran a parallel civil investigation and went to federal court to compel testimony from a family member; and when the Department of Justice tried to keep the whole file dark, a federal judge ordered part of it opened over the Department’s objection. What did not happen is a charge: the criminal investigation closed in January 2021 with no prosecution. The timing also matters to the sweeping version of the claim — the trades that the court record actually concerns are dated 13 February 2020, not January, and the record read here concerns one senator. The filings of the other members named in 2020 coverage were not read, and nothing is asserted about them here.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Stocks worth between $628,000 and $1.72 million sold by Senator Burr and his wife on 13 February 2020, as disclosed under the STOCK Act. Pandemic briefings received shortly before, in his capacity as a member of the Senate HELP Committee. A sealed warrant for his cellphone granted on 13 May 2020, in an investigation the government later described as directed to "whether Senator Burr sold or purchased stock based on non-public information relating to the COVID-19 pandemic that he received by virtue of his position as a United States Senator". An SEC investigation running in parallel, disclosed in its own October 2021 filing, which also recorded telephone records among Burr, his brother-in-law Gerald Fauth and their brokers, and a declaration that prosecutors had told Fauth’s counsel his criminal investigation was closed. A Justice Department review closed in January 2021 without charges. And a court order of 29 August 2022 unsealing the parts of the warrant affidavit that make the probable-cause allegations, precisely because no charge was ever brought on them. What remains sealed is what the allegations rested on; what is settled is that no court was ever asked to decide whether they were true.

citations.title: In re Application of Los Angeles Times Communications LLC to Unseal Court Records, Misc. Action No. 21-16 (BAH) (D.D.C., Chief Judge Beryl A. Howell, Memorandum Opinion and Order, 29 August 2022)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full in a browser on CourtListener (the CourtListener API returns 401 to unauthenticated requests and the plain page returns an empty 202 to scripts). The opinion states that "On May 13, 2020, the government presented, and this Court granted under seal, a warrant to search the cellphone of Senator Burr as part of a now closed investigation into allegations of insider training and securities fraud, in violation of 15 U.S.C. § 78j(b) and 18 U.S.C. § 1348, respectively" (the typographical slip for "trading" is the court's). Quoting the government's own motion, it records that the government "sought to determine whether Senator Burr sold or purchased stock based on non-public information relating to the COVID-19 pandemic that he received by virtue of his position as a United States Senator, in violation of the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act ('STOCK Act'), codified at 15 U.S.C. §§ 78j(b), 78u-1(g)." It quotes the D.C. Circuit's factual summary that "On February 13, 2020, Senator Richard Burr and his wife sold stocks valued between $628,000 and $1.72 million, as disclosed in mandatory Senate filings", that the market then fell sharply, and that "shortly before those sales, Senator Burr had received briefings on the pandemic in his capacity as a Senator and member of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions". It records Senator Burr's January 2021 statement in full as reported: "Tonight, the Department of Justice informed me that it has concluded its review of my personal financial transactions conducted early last year. The case is now closed." It records that for over a year of litigation "DOJ never publicly recognized the existence of either the search warrant materials or any DOJ investigation into Senator Burr", that the district court had therefore to treat the warrant as "hypothesized", and that only on 24 May 2022, after the D.C. Circuit's remand, did DOJ notify the court that it "now acknowledges the existence of the Materials". The disposition: the government's motion for continued sealing was "GRANTED IN PART AND DENIED IN PART"; redactions protecting third-party privacy and law-enforcement techniques were retained, while "DOJ's proposed redactions intended to preserve the due process interests of investigative targets against whom the probable cause allegations in the warrant were made without any criminal charges being brought must be disclosed", with specified paragraphs of the supporting affidavit ordered unsealed by 5 September 2022. The opinion twice describes the matter as a "closed investigation that resulted in no prosecution of former Senator Burr". It makes no finding that any law was broken; it decides only what the public may see.

citations.title: In re Application of Los Angeles Times Communications LLC to Unseal Court Records, No. 21-5128, 28 F.4th 292 (D.C. Cir., argued 2 February 2022, decided 18 March 2022)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the court's own opinions server and read as extracted text. Opinion for the court by Circuit Judge Rogers. It opens the facts: "On February 13, 2020, Senator Richard Burr and his wife sold stocks valued between $628,000 and $1.72 million, as disclosed in mandatory Senate filings. Soon after, the stock market fell sharply as news about the COVID-19 pandemic spread. Because, shortly before those sales, Senator Burr had received briefings on the pandemic in his capacity as a Senator and member of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, the February 13 trades quickly garnered media scrutiny and public attention." It records the L.A. Times report of 13 May 2020 that a search warrant had been served and the Senator's cellphone seized, sourced to "a law enforcement official speaking on condition of anonymity", and that "Eight months later, Senator Burr issued a public statement noting that the investigation into the stock transactions had been closed." On the parallel civil matter it records that the SEC applied in the Southern District of New York for an order compelling compliance with an investigative subpoena issued to the Senator's brother-in-law Gerald Fauth (SEC v. Fauth, No. 1:21-mc-00787, filed 22 October 2021), that in its memorandum of law "the SEC disclosed that it was investigating stock trades by Senator Burr and Mr. Fauth, and that its investigation paralleled an investigation by the Justice Department", that the filing "also disclosed some of the underlying facts, including records of phone calls among Burr, Fauth, and their brokers", and that a declaration by Fauth's counsel "recounted a conversation in which Justice Department prosecutors stated that the criminal investigation of Fauth was closed." The court remanded for reconsideration of the common-law access analysis under United States v. Hubbard. It decided a question of public access only, reached no view on the merits of any allegation, and did not reach the First Amendment argument.

citations.title: Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act of 2012 (STOCK Act), Pub. L. 112-105, 126 Stat. 291 (4 April 2012) — sections 4 and 6
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. Section 4(a), "Affirmation of nonexemption", provides that "Members of Congress and employees of Congress are not exempt from the insider trading prohibitions arising under the securities laws, including section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder." Section 4(b) states that its purpose "is to affirm a duty arising from a relationship of trust and confidence owed by each Member of Congress and each employee of Congress", and amends section 21A of the Securities Exchange Act by adding subsection (g): each Member or employee of Congress "owes a duty arising from a relationship of trust and confidence to the Congress, the United States Government, and the citizens of the United States with respect to material, nonpublic information derived from such person's position as a Member of Congress or employee of Congress or gained from the performance of such person's official responsibilities." Section 6, "Prompt reporting of financial transactions", amends section 103 of the Ethics in Government Act of 1978 to require a report of a covered transaction "Not later than 30 days after receiving notification of any transaction required to be reported under section 102(a)(5)(B), but in no case later than 45 days after such transaction". Section 3 directs the ethics committees of both chambers to issue interpretive guidance clarifying that nonpublic information derived from the office may not be used "as a means for making a private profit". The Act creates the disclosure duty; it does not itself make any finding about any filer.
